steps.body: deg A = 4, deg B = 3, deg C = 2, deg D = 4, deg E = 3, deg F = 4. Removing C's two edges, B–C and C–F, isolates C. So the min-cut is at most 2.

steps.title: No bridge
steps.body:
Every edge lies on a cycle. For example, B–C and C–F lie on B–C–F–A–B, A–E, E–F and D–E lie on A–E–F–A and A–E–D–A, and B–D and D–F lie on B–D–F–A–B. A graph where every edge lies on a cycle has no bridge, so no single edge is a cut.

Min-cut cardinality = **2**.

cse-1999-b-53-b.verification: Removing any one edge leaves the graph connected, and the set $\{B\text{–}C, C\text{–}F\}$ disconnects it.

cse-1999-b-53-c.approach: Every vertex has degree at least $k$, because its incident edges form a cut. Then apply the handshaking lemma.

steps.title: Degree bound
steps.body: Removing all edges at a vertex $v$ isolates $v$, assuming $n\ge 2$. So these $\deg(v)$ edges form a cut, and $\deg(v)\ge k$ for every $v$.

steps.title: Handshaking
steps.body: $$2|E| = \sum_{v}\deg(v) \ge nk \implies |E| \ge \frac{nk}{2}.$$

answer.value: Every vertex has degree ≥ k (its incident edges form a cut), so 2|E| = Σdeg ≥ nk.

cse-1999-b-53-c.verification: Check on the given graph: $n=6$, $k=2$, and $|E|=10\ge 6$.

cse-1999-b-54-a.approach: A single counterexample answers this. Choose $A=\Sigma^*$, which absorbs any $B$.

steps.title: Counterexample
steps.body: Let $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$, $A=\Sigma^*$ (regular), and $B=\{a^nb^n\mid n\ge0\}$ (not regular).

steps.title: Check
steps.body: $A\cup B=\Sigma^*$, which is regular, but $B$ is not regular. So **no**, $B$ need not be regular.

pitfalls: Closure under union goes one way only: regular ∪ regular is regular. The converse does not hold.
cse-1999-b-54-a.verification: $B\subseteq\Sigma^*$, so the union is $\Sigma^*$. $B$ fails the pumping lemma.

cse-1999-b-54-b.approach: Reduce both conditions to emptiness tests on product DFAs. $L_1\subsetneq L_2$ holds iff $L_1\cap\overline{L_2}=\emptyset$ and $L_2\cap\overline{L_1}\neq\emptyset$.

steps.title: Make DFAs
steps.body: If $M_1$ or $M_2$ is an NFA, determinize it with the subset construction and make it complete by adding a dead state. Complementing a DFA means swapping final and non-final states.

steps.title: Subset test
steps.body: Build the product DFA for $L(M_1)\cap\overline{L(M_2)}$: states are pairs $(p,q)$, and a pair is final iff $p\in F_1$ and $q\notin F_2$. Run BFS/DFS from $(s_1,s_2)$. If no final pair is reachable, then $L(M_1)\subseteq L(M_2)$.

steps.title: Strictness test
steps.body: Similarly build $L(M_2)\cap\overline{L(M_1)}$ (final iff $q\in F_2$ and $p\notin F_1$). If a final pair **is** reachable, then $L(M_2)\not\subseteq L(M_1)$.

steps.title: Decision
steps.body: Answer YES iff the first product is empty and the second is non-empty. Both are graph-reachability problems on at most $|Q_1|\cdot|Q_2|$ states, so the algorithm always halts.

answer.value: Test L(M1) ∩ ¬L(M2) = ∅ and L(M2) ∩ ¬L(M1) ≠ ∅ using product DFAs and reachability.

pitfalls: A DFA must be complete before its final states are swapped, otherwise the complement is wrong.
cse-1999-b-54-b.verification: Equivalent formulation: $L_1\subsetneq L_2$ iff $L_1\subseteq L_2$ and $L_1\neq L_2$. The second condition is exactly the non-emptiness of $L_2\setminus L_1$.

cse-1999-b-55.approach: Use the CFL pumping lemma with $s=0^p1^pc0^p1^p$. A pumped window $vwx$ has length at most $p$, so it cannot change both copies consistently.

steps.title: Setup
steps.body: Assume $L$ is context-free with pumping length $p$. Take $s=0^p1^pc0^p1^p\in L$, with $|s|\ge p$. Write $s=uvwxy$ with $|vwx|\le p$, $|vx|\ge1$, and $uv^iwx^iy\in L$ for all $i\ge0$.

steps.title: c inside v or x
steps.body: Then $uv^0wx^0y$ has no $c$, but every string of $L$ contains exactly one $c$. Contradiction. So $c$ lies in $u$, $w$ or $y$.

steps.title: vx entirely on one side
steps.body: Pumping down to $i=0$ changes only the left half or only the right half. The two halves then have different lengths, so the result is not of the form $xcx$. Contradiction.

steps.title: vwx straddles c
steps.body:
Here $c\in w$, and since $|vwx|\le p$, $v$ lies within the $1^p$ before $c$ and $x$ within the $0^p$ after $c$. Pumping down gives $0^p1^{p-j}c0^{p-l}1^p$ with $j+l\ge1$. If both halves had the same length, then $j=l\ge1$, but then the left half begins with $0^p$ while the right half begins with only $p-l<p$ zeros. So the halves differ. Contradiction.

Hence $L$ is **not** context-free.

answer.value: Pump $s = 0^p1^pc0^p1^p$ with the CFL pumping lemma.

pitfalls: Choosing $0^pc0^p$ fails, because it can be pumped symmetrically around $c$. The $1^p$ blocks are what defeat the straddling case.
cse-1999-b-55.verification: For the straddling case with $j=l=1$ (and $p\ge 2$): the left half is $0^p1^{p-1}$ and the right half is $0^{p-1}1^p$. These are unequal.

cse-1999-b-56.approach: Use the order constraints. The smallest is $A[1][1]$. The 2nd is $A[1][2]$ or $A[2][1]$. The 3rd is the loser of that comparison or the next element on the winner's line. That gives two comparisons on every path.

steps.title: 1st smallest
steps.body: Rows and columns ascend, so $A[1][1]$ is the minimum. It needs **0 comparisons**.

steps.title: 2nd smallest
steps.body: Every other element is at least $A[1][2]$ or at least $A[2][1]$. So the 2nd smallest is $\min(A[1][2],A[2][1])$, which takes **1 comparison** and is the root of the tree.

steps.title: 3rd smallest
steps.body:
If $A[1][2]<A[2][1]$, the candidates are $A[2][1]$ and $A[1][3]$. $A[2][2]$ is not a candidate because $A[2][2]>A[2][1]$. Compare them.
If $A[2][1]<A[1][2]$, the candidates are $A[1][2]$ and $A[3][1]$. Compare them.

Decision tree:
```text
                 A12 < A21 ?
              yes /        \ no
   2nd = A12     /          \    2nd = A21
          A21 < A13 ?        A12 < A31 ?
          /       \          /       \
   3rd=A21    3rd=A13   3rd=A12   3rd=A31
```
(1st = A11 on every leaf.)

steps.title: Optimality
steps.body: One comparison cannot decide both the 2nd and the 3rd smallest, because 3 orderings of the candidates remain possible. So **2 comparisons** is the minimum.

answer.value: 2 comparisons: 1st = A[1][1]; compare A[1][2] with A[2][1]; then compare the loser with the winner's successor (A[1][3] or A[3][1]).

pitfalls: $A[2][2]$ can never be the 3rd smallest, since it is greater than both $A[1][2]$ and $A[2][1]$.
cse-1999-b-56.verification: Tried $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\\7&8&9\end{bmatrix}$: $2<4$, then $3<4$, so the 3rd is 3. Correct.

cse-1999-b-57.approach: Compute the integer part with $L.val=2L_1.val+B.val$. For the fraction, also synthesize the length of $L$ and divide the fraction digits' integer value by $2^{len}$.

steps.title: Bits and lists
steps.body:
| Production | Semantic rules |
|---|---|
| $B\to0$ | $B.val=0$ |
| $B\to1$ | $B.val=1$ |
| $L\to B$ | $L.val=B.val;\ L.len=1$ |
| $L\to L_1B$ | $L.val=2\cdot L_1.val+B.val;\ L.len=L_1.len+1$ |

steps.title: Start symbol
steps.body:
| Production | Semantic rule |
|---|---|
| $S\to L$ | $S.val=L.val$ |
| $S\to L_1.L_2$ | $S.val=L_1.val+L_2.val/2^{L_2.len}$ |

All attributes are synthesized, so the definition is S-attributed.

answer.value: S→L1.L2: S.val = L1.val + L2.val/2^{L2.len}; S→L: S.val = L.val; L→L1 B: L.val = 2·L1.val + B.val, L.len = L1.len+1; L→B: L.val = B.val, L.len = 1; B→0: B.val=0; B→1: B.val=1.

pitfalls: Without the $len$ attribute the fraction cannot be weighted, because $.1$ and $.001$ are different values.

cse-1999-b-58-a.approach: Use the assumption that HALTS is total (it always answers), then check both branches of FUNNY.

steps.title: Evaluating the condition
steps.body: By hypothesis, HALTS terminates on every input and returns TRUE or FALSE. So the test HALTS($f\,f$) always finishes.

steps.title: Both branches
steps.body: If TRUE, then $f\,f$ terminates, so evaluating $f\,f$ and negating it terminates too. If FALSE, FUNNY returns TRUE immediately. Either way, FUNNY($f$) terminates for every $f$.

answer.value: HALTS always terminates; if it says TRUE then f f terminates so not(f f) terminates, otherwise FUNNY returns TRUE immediately.

cse-1999-b-58-a.verification: Both branches are covered and each one terminates.

cse-1999-b-58-b.approach: Use diagonalization: apply FUNNY to itself. By (a) the call halts, and then its own definition makes it equal its own negation.

steps.title: Self-application
steps.body: Suppose HALTS exists. Consider FUNNY(FUNNY). By (a) it terminates, so HALTS(FUNNY FUNNY) = TRUE.

steps.title: Contradiction
steps.body: Then by definition FUNNY(FUNNY) = not(FUNNY FUNNY). A terminating Boolean computation cannot equal its own negation. So HALTS cannot exist, and termination is undecidable.

answer.value: Consider FUNNY(FUNNY): since it halts, HALTS(FUNNY FUNNY) = TRUE, so FUNNY(FUNNY) = not(FUNNY(FUNNY)) — a contradiction.

cse-1999-b-58-b.verification: The only assumption used, besides the definition of FUNNY, was that HALTS exists. So that assumption is false.

cse-1999-b-59-a.approach: Write the recurrence. The recursion runs $n$ levels deep, and each level does a constant amount of control work plus a call to B. That constant work dominates.

steps.title: Recurrence
steps.body: $T(1)=O(1)$ for call A. For $n>1$: $T(n)=T(n-1)+O(1/n)+c$, where $c$ is the constant cost of the test and the call in each activation.

steps.title: Unroll
steps.body:
$$T(n)=\sum_{k=2}^{n}\left(c+\frac1k\right)+O(1)=c(n-1)+(H_n-1)+O(1).$$
$H_n=\Theta(\log n)$, so $T(n)=\Theta(n)+\Theta(\log n)=O(n)$.

pitfalls: If you count only the time spent inside A and B, you get $1+\sum 1/k = \Theta(\log n)$. But the $n$ recursive calls themselves cost $\Theta(n)$.
cse-1999-b-59-a.verification: The call depth is exactly $n$ (what(n), what(n−1), …, what(1)), so the total is at least $n$ constant-time activations.

cse-1999-b-59-b.approach: You cannot reach p's predecessor in O(1), so insert the new node *after* p and swap the data: the new node takes p's old data and p takes D. In list order D now sits just before the old contents of p.

steps.title: Why the obvious way fails
steps.body: Inserting before $p$ normally needs the predecessor of $p$, and finding it means walking from the head — $O(n)$. A singly linked list has no back pointer.

steps.title: Insert after p, then swap data
Cost
steps.body: One allocation and four assignments, no traversal, so the time is $O(1)$ whatever the list length.

answer.value: Allocate q; q→data = p→data; q→next = p→next; p→next = q; p→data = D. This puts D just before the old contents of p in O(1).

pitfalls: Searching for the predecessor makes it O(n).
Forgetting to copy p's old data into the new node loses that value.
If other pointers refer to p's node (not just its data), they now see D — the trick moves data, not nodes.
cse-1999-b-59-b.verification: Traced on the list 1 → 5 → 9 with p at 5 and D = 7: after the code the list reads 1 → 7 → 5 → 9.

cse-1999-b-60-a.approach: Strong induction on the height h. Split on the root: no child, one child, two children. A one-child root adds nothing to either count; a two-child root adds one full node and the leaf counts of both subtrees add.

steps.title: Claim and notation
steps.body: For a non-empty binary tree $T$ let $F(T)$ = number of full nodes (2 children) and $L(T)$ = number of leaves. Claim: $F(T)+1 = L(T)$. Induct on the height $h$.

steps.title: Base case h = 0
steps.body: The tree is a single node: it is a leaf and not full, so $F=0$, $L=1$, and $0+1=1$. ✓

steps.title: Root with one child
steps.body:
Assume the claim for all trees of height $< h$, and let $T$ have height $h \ge 1$. If the root has one child, its subtree $T_1$ has height $h-1$. The root is neither full nor a leaf, so
$$F(T)+1 = F(T_1)+1 = L(T_1) = L(T).$$

steps.title: Root with two children
steps.body:
Subtrees $T_1, T_2$ have height $\le h-1$, so $F(T_i)+1 = L(T_i)$. The root is full, so
$$F(T)+1 = \big(F(T_1)+F(T_2)+1\big)+1 = \big(F(T_1)+1\big)+\big(F(T_2)+1\big) = L(T_1)+L(T_2) = L(T).$$
By induction the claim holds for every height. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: By induction on height: base h = 0 gives 0 + 1 = 1; a one-child root changes neither count; a two-child root gives F + 1 = (F1 + 1) + (F2 + 1) = L1 + L2 = L. So full nodes + 1 = leaves.

pitfalls: Forgetting the one-child case — binary trees need not be full.
Using ordinary induction on h−1 only: one subtree of a two-child root can be shorter than h−1, so use strong induction (heights ≤ h−1).
cse-1999-b-60-a.verification: Checked on a 5-node tree whose root has 2 children, one of which has 2 leaf children: F = 2, L = 3.

cse-1999-b-60-b.approach: Insert each key at the next free leaf position and bubble it up while it is smaller than its parent. To delete the root, move the last leaf to the root and sift it down, always swapping with the smaller child.

steps.title: Delete the root
steps.body:
Remove 1 and move the last leaf 3 to the root: $[3,4,2,7,5,6]$. Children of 3 are 4 and 2; the smaller is 2 and $3>2$, swap → $[2,4,3,7,5,6]$. Now 3's only child is 6 and $3<6$, stop.

Result (level order): $2;\ 4, 3;\ 7, 5, 6$.

answer.value: After insertions: [1, 4, 2, 7, 5, 6, 3]; after deleting the root: [2, 4, 3, 7, 5, 6] (level order).

pitfalls: Building the heap with bottom-up heapify gives a different (also valid) heap — the question asks for successive insertions.
When sifting down, swap with the smaller child, not always the left one.
cse-1999-b-60-b.verification: Every parent ≤ its children in both final arrays: 1≤4,2; 4≤7,5; 2≤6,3 and 2≤4,3; 4≤7,5; 3≤6.

cse-1999-b-61.approach: Fill a space-time table: an instruction enters a stage once it has finished the previous stage and the previous instruction has left that stage. Writing finish times as $t_{i,s} = \max(t_{i,s-1}, t_{i-1,s}) + c_{i,s}$, the answer is the W finish time of I5.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body:
Let $t_{i,s}$ be the cycle at which instruction $i$ finishes stage $s$ and $c_{i,s}$ its cycle count. Then
$$t_{i,s} = \max(t_{i,s-1},\ t_{i-1,s}) + c_{i,s}$$
(start after your own previous stage and after the previous instruction frees the stage).

pitfalls: Using (k + n − 1) × max stage time = 8 × 3 = 24 assumes a synchronous pipeline clocked by the slowest stage; here each instruction's per-stage cycle counts are given.
Adding all cycle counts (sequential execution) gives 36, not the pipelined time.
cse-1999-b-61.verification: Re-ran the schedule with no inter-stage buffers (an instruction holds its stage until the next one is free): I4 waits in D until 10, I5 decodes 10–12, executes 13 and writes 14–15 — still 15 cycles. The '-' cells in the diagram are waiting cycles.

cse-1999-b-62-a.approach: An implication is false only when its premise is true and its conclusion false. Make $q \Rightarrow p$ false ($q=T, p=F$) and check that the premise $\sim p \vee q$ is then true.

steps.title: Falsify the conclusion
steps.body: $q \Rightarrow p$ is false only for $q = T,\ p = F$.

steps.title: Check the premise
steps.body: With $p=F$: $\sim p = T$, so $\sim p \vee q = T$. The formula becomes $T \Rightarrow F = F$.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: An assignment ($p=F, q=T$) makes the formula false, so it is not a tautology.

answer.value: p = F, q = T: (∼p ∨ q) = T and (q ⇒ p) = F, so the formula is F; hence not a tautology.

pitfalls: Checking only rows with p = T, where the conclusion q ⇒ p is always true.
cse-1999-b-62-a.verification: Full truth table (p,q): TT→T, TF→T, FT→F, FF→T; exactly one false row.

cse-1999-b-62-b.approach: A tautology is true under every truth assignment, and a disjunction is true as soon as one disjunct is true. So $A \vee B$ is true under every assignment.

steps.title: Take any assignment
steps.body: Let $v$ be any truth assignment to the variables of $A$ and $B$. Since $A$ is a tautology, $v(A) = T$ (values of variables outside $A$ do not matter).

steps.title: Disjunction
steps.body: $v(A \vee B) = v(A) \vee v(B) = T \vee v(B) = T$. As $v$ was arbitrary, $A \vee B$ is true under every assignment, i.e. a tautology. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: Under every assignment v, v(A) = T, so v(A ∨ B) = T ∨ v(B) = T; therefore A ∨ B is a tautology.

pitfalls: Trying to reason about B's truth value — it is irrelevant.
cse-1999-b-62-b.verification: Equivalently A ≡ T, and T ∨ B ≡ T by the domination law.

cse-1999-b-63.approach: Trace the body y := y+1; z := z+x for each mechanism. Under reference, y and z are both aliases of a; under copy-restore they are separate copies written back to a on return, so the last write-back wins.

steps.title: Call by value
steps.body: $x=5,\ y=2,\ z=2$ are local copies. $y=3,\ z=2+5=7$, but nothing goes back to $a$. **print(a) → 2**.

steps.title: Call by reference
steps.body:
$x$ refers to a temporary holding $a+b=5$; $y$ and $z$ both refer to $a$.

- $y := y+1$ → $a = 2+1 = 3$
- $z := z+x$ → $a = 3+5 = 8$

**print(a) → 8**.

steps.title: Call by copy-restore
steps.body:
Copy in: $x=5,\ y=2,\ z=2$. Body: $y=3$, $z=2+5=7$. Copy out left to right: $a := y = 3$, then $a := z = 7$. **print(a) → 7**.

(If results were copied back right to left, $a$ would end as 3; the usual left-to-right convention gives 7.)

pitfalls: Under reference, z sees the updated a (3), not the original 2.
Under copy-restore, z works on its own copy (2), so z = 7, not 8.
a+b is an expression: by reference it binds to a temporary, so no write reaches b.
cse-1999-b-63.verification: Re-traced each case with a memory table for a, b and the formals; b stays 3 in every case.

cse-1999-b-65-a.approach: SHR then SHL clears the lowest bit, so comparing with the saved copy tests whether the LSB was 1; R3 is incremented in that case, and the extra SHR at Y moves to the next bit. Trace with R1 = 5 = 101₂.

steps.title: What one iteration does
steps.body: R2 := R1; R1 := (R1 >> 1) << 1 (LSB cleared). If R2 ≠ R1 the LSB was 1 → R3++. Then at Y, R1 := R1 >> 1, i.e. the original R1 shifted right by one.

pitfalls: Forgetting the SHR at Y, which runs on both paths.
Reporting R2 — the question asks for R1 and R3.
cse-1999-b-65-a.verification: 5 = 101₂ has two 1-bits, matching R3 = 2; the loop exits only when R1 = 0.

cse-1999-b-65-b.approach: Each iteration examines the current least significant bit (SHR/SHL clears it; inequality means it was 1), increments R3 for a 1, and shifts R1 right. The loop stops when R1 = 0, so R3 counts the 1-bits of n.

steps.title: One iteration
steps.body: With $R1 = r$: $R2 = r$, $R1 = 2\lfloor r/2 \rfloor$. $R2 \ne R1$ iff $r$ is odd (LSB = 1), and then R3 increases by 1. At Y, $R1 = \lfloor r/2 \rfloor$.

steps.title: Invariant
steps.body: $R3 + (\text{number of 1s in } R1) = \text{number of 1s in } n$ holds initially ($R3=0, R1=n$) and is preserved by every iteration. When the loop ends $R1 = 0$, so R3 = number of 1s in the binary representation of $n$.

answer.value: The number of 1s in the binary representation of n.

pitfalls: Answering ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 (the number of bits) — iterations with a 0 bit skip the INC.
This assumes logical shifts (n treated as unsigned).
cse-1999-b-65-b.verification: n = 5 (101₂) gives 2, as in part (a); n = 7 gives 3; n = 8 gives 1.

cse-1999-b-66.approach: Two 1K×4 chips side by side make a 1K×8 bank (one supplies D0–D3, the other D4–D7); two banks give 2K×8. A0–A9 go to every chip, A10 picks the bank, and A15–A11 = 00010 with IO/M̄ = 0 enables the block.

|---|---|---|---|
| 1000H–13FFH | 0 0 0 1 0 | 0 | 000H–3FFH |
| 1400H–17FFH | 0 0 0 1 0 | 1 | 000H–3FFH |

So A15–A11 = 00010 is fixed, A10 selects the 1K bank, and A9–A0 address a location inside a chip.

steps.title: Chip organisation
steps.body:
| Chip | Data lines | Addresses |
|---|---|---|
| C1 | D0–D3 | 1000H–13FFH (bank 0) |
| C2 | D4–D7 | 1000H–13FFH (bank 0) |
| C3 | D0–D3 | 1400H–17FFH (bank 1) |

steps.title: Chip-select logic
steps.body:
$$\overline{CS}_{0} = \overline{\overline{A_{15}}\,\overline{A_{14}}\,\overline{A_{13}}\,A_{12}\,\overline{A_{11}}\,\overline{A_{10}}\,\overline{IO/\overline{M}}}, \qquad \overline{CS}_{1} = \overline{\overline{A_{15}}\,\overline{A_{14}}\,\overline{A_{13}}\,A_{12}\,\overline{A_{11}}\,A_{10}\,\overline{IO/\overline{M}}}$$
C1 and C2 share $\overline{CS}_{0}$; C3 and C4 share $\overline{CS}_{1}$.

With a 74138 3-to-8 decoder: select inputs $C\,B\,A = A_{12}\,A_{11}\,A_{10}$, $G_1 = 1$, $\overline{G_{2A}} = A_{15}+A_{14}$, $\overline{G_{2B}} = A_{13}+IO/\overline{M}$; output $\overline{Y_4}$ (100) → bank 0, $\overline{Y_5}$ (101) → bank 1.

answer.value: Two banks of two 1K×4 chips (low/high nibble); A0–A9 to all chips; bank 0 at 1000–13FF (A10=0), bank 1 at 1400–17FF (A10=1); decode A15–A11 = 00010 with IO/M̄ = 0 to form the CS̄ signals.

pitfalls: Putting both chips of a bank on the same data nibble — they must split D0–D3 and D4–D7.
Leaving IO/M̄ out of the decode lets I/O cycles enable the memory.
Partial decoding (ignoring A13–A15) creates mirror images of the block elsewhere in the address space.
cse-1999-b-66.verification: 1000H → A15–A10 = 000100 → bank 0, offset 000H; 17FFH → 000101 → bank 1, offset 3FFH; 1800H → A11 = 1 → no chip selected.

cse-1999-b-67-a.approach: Each segment is $2^{16}/8 = 2^{13}$ bytes. With page size $2^p$, a segment's page table has $2^{13-p}$ two-byte entries, i.e. $2^{14-p}$ bytes; require this to fit in one page.

steps.title: Segment size
steps.body: $2^{16}/8 = 2^{13}$ bytes per segment.

steps.title: Page-table size vs page size
steps.body:
Page size $2^p$ ⇒ $2^{13-p}$ pages per segment ⇒ page table $= 2^{13-p} \times 2 = 2^{14-p}$ bytes.
$$2^{14-p} \le 2^p \iff 14 \le 2p \iff p \ge 7.$$
Minimum page size $= 2^7 = 128$ bytes.

pitfalls: Using the whole 2¹⁶ address space instead of one segment: 2^{17−p} ≤ 2^p gives p ≥ 9 (512 bytes) — but the page table is per segment.
cse-1999-b-67-a.verification: p = 7: 2⁶ entries × 2 B = 128 B = one page ✓; p = 6: 2⁷ × 2 = 256 B > 64 B ✗.

cse-1999-b-67-b.approach: The TLB is indexed by the virtual page number (segment + page). With 512-byte pages the VPN has 16 − 9 = 7 bits; 16 direct-mapped entries use 4 index bits, leaving 3 tag bits.

steps.title: Virtual page number
steps.body: Offset $= \log_2 512 = 9$ bits, so VPN $= 16-9 = 7$ bits (3 segment bits + 4 page bits).

steps.title: Split for a direct-mapped TLB
steps.body: 16 entries ⇒ index $= \log_2 16 = 4$ bits. Tag $= 7 - 4 = 3$ bits.

pitfalls: Subtracting the index from the full 16-bit address (giving 12) — the page offset is never looked up in the TLB.
cse-1999-b-67-b.verification: 7 VPN bits = 3 tag + 4 index; 2³ × 2⁴ = 128 virtual pages = 2¹⁶ / 2⁹ ✓.

cse-1999-b-67-c.approach: A 2-byte PTE has 16 bits. The frame number needs 16 − 9 = 7 bits (physical space 2¹⁶, pages of 512 B); valid, protection and dirty take 1 + 3 + 1 = 5; the rest is free for aging.
pitfalls: Forgetting the frame-number field and answering 11.

cse-1999-b-68-a.approach: Spin until TSET returns 0 (the flag was free; TSET has already set it to 1, so we own the lock). On exit simply clear the flag.

steps.title: Entry code
steps.body:
```
ENTRY: TSET R, flag     ; R := flag, flag := 1 (atomic)
       CMP  R, 0
       JNZ  ENTRY       ; flag was 1 -> someone inside, retry
       ; critical region
```

steps.title: Exit code
steps.body:
```
EXIT:  MOV  flag, 0      ; release the lock
```
flag starts at 0. Because TSET reads and sets in one atomic step, only one process can see R = 0 while flag goes 0 → 1.

answer.value: Entry: L: TSET R, flag; if R ≠ 0 goto L. Exit: flag := 0.

pitfalls: Reading flag and setting it in two separate instructions — that loses atomicity.
Looping while R = 0 (inverted test).
cse-1999-b-68-a.verification: Two processes racing: the first TSET returns 0 and sets flag = 1; the second gets 1 and spins until the exit code stores 0.

cse-1999-b-68-b.approach: The test of count and the sleep are not one atomic step. A wakeup sent between a process's test and its sleep is lost, after which each process waits for the other.

steps.title: Interleaving
steps.body:
| # | Consumer | Producer | count |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | tests count = 0, decides to sleep; preempted before sleeping | | 0 |
| 2 | | produces; count ≠ 1, places item | 0 |
| 3 | | count := 1; wakeup(Consumer) — consumer not yet asleep, **wakeup lost** | 1 |
| 4 | | produces next item; count = 1 → sleep | 1 |
| 5 | resumes and executes sleep | | 1 |

steps.title: Result
steps.body: The producer sleeps waiting for the consumer to empty the buffer, and the consumer sleeps waiting for a wakeup that already happened. Neither will ever wake the other, so both sleep forever.

answer.value: Lost wakeup: consumer tests count = 0, is preempted before sleeping; producer fills buffer, sets count = 1, wakeup is lost; consumer sleeps; producer then finds count = 1 and sleeps.

pitfalls: Making the test of count atomic does not help — the test and the sleep together must be atomic (semaphores fix this by remembering wakeups).
cse-1999-b-68-b.verification: In the final state count = 1 (an item is waiting) yet both processes are blocked — a deadlock.

cse-1999-b-69.approach: Count leaves first: the fullest tree has every node with 2m−1 children; the sparsest has a root with 2 children and every other internal node with m. Each leaf holds between m−1 and 2m−2 records (a node with c children holds c−1 keys), so multiply.

steps.title: Number of leaves
steps.body:
Leaves are at depth $h$.

- Maximum: every node has $2m-1$ children ⇒ $(2m-1)^h$ leaves.
- Minimum: the root has 2 children and every other internal node $m$ ⇒ $2\,m^{h-1}$ leaves.

steps.title: Records per leaf
steps.body: A node with $c$ children holds $c-1$ keys and $m \le c \le 2m-1$, so a non-root node (leaves included) holds between $m-1$ and $2m-2$ records.

steps.title: Records in the leaf level
steps.body:
$$\max = (2m-1)^h\,(2m-2), \qquad \min = 2\,m^{h-1}\,(m-1).$$
If 'records in the leaf nodes' is read as the number of leaf nodes, the bounds are $(2m-1)^h$ and $2m^{h-1}$.

answer.value: Leaf nodes: max (2m−1)^h, min 2m^{h−1}; with m−1 … 2m−2 keys per leaf, records: max (2m−1)^h(2m−2), min 2m^{h−1}(m−1).

pitfalls: Giving the root m children in the minimum case — the root only needs 2.
Counting keys in internal nodes when the question asks about leaves.
cse-1999-b-69.verification: m = 2 (a 2-3 tree), h = 1: leaves between 2 and 3, records between 2·1 = 2 and 3·2 = 6 — consistent with a 2-3 tree of height 1.

cse-1999-b-70-a.approach: Join EMP and DEPT on Dept-no, then filter on Location and Salary and project the name.

steps.title: Query
steps.body:
```sql
SELECT E."Employee-name"
FROM   EMP E, DEPT D
WHERE  E."Dept-no" = D."Dept-no"
  AND  D.Location = 'Calcutta'
  AND  E.Salary > 50000;
```
(Hyphenated column names are quoted so they are not parsed as subtraction.)

steps.title: Why it works
steps.body: The join pairs each employee with their department; the two conditions keep only Calcutta departments and salaries above 50,000.

answer.value: SELECT E.Employee-name FROM EMP E, DEPT D WHERE E.Dept-no = D.Dept-no AND D.Location = 'Calcutta' AND E.Salary > 50000;

pitfalls: Omitting the join condition gives a Cartesian product.
Using ≥ instead of > for 'greater than'.
cse-1999-b-70-a.verification: The nested form WHERE Dept-no IN (SELECT Dept-no FROM DEPT WHERE Location = 'Calcutta') AND Salary > 50000 returns the same names.

cse-1999-b-70-b.approach: Filter rows with WHERE before grouping, then GROUP BY Dept-no and COUNT.

steps.title: Query
steps.body:
```sql
SELECT "Dept-no", COUNT(*)
FROM   EMP
WHERE  Salary > 100000
GROUP BY "Dept-no";
```

steps.title: Why WHERE, not HAVING
steps.body: The condition is on each employee's salary, so it filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters whole groups.

answer.value: SELECT Dept-no, COUNT(*) FROM EMP WHERE Salary > 100000 GROUP BY Dept-no;

pitfalls: HAVING Salary > 100000 is invalid (Salary is not grouped).
Departments with no such employee are omitted; listing them with 0 needs an outer join with DEPT.
cse-1999-b-70-b.verification: Each group's COUNT(*) counts only rows that passed the salary filter.
